title: PriorityQueue vs sorted list: when to use each
shortTitle: PriorityQueue vs sorted list: when to use each?
keyPoints: PriorityQueue is a min-heap: only the head is guaranteed to be the minimum/maximum element; iteration order is NOT sorted
add() and poll() are O(log n); peek() is O(1) because the minimum is always at the root of the heap
A sorted list (ArrayList + sort) maintains all elements in order but insertion while maintaining sort is O(n)
TreeSet provides O(log n) add/remove/contains with sorted iteration, but does not allow duplicates
Use PriorityQueue when you repeatedly need the next highest/lowest priority element (task scheduling, event processing)
Use sorted list or TreeSet when you need all elements in sorted order for reports or range queries
PriorityQueue allows duplicates; TreeSet does not

s1_definition.oneliner: PriorityQueue is a min-heap where only the head is guaranteed to be the smallest element; use it for repeated min/max extraction. Use a sorted list or TreeSet when you need all elements in order.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **PriorityQueue** is backed by a binary min-heap; the smallest element (by natural order or Comparator) is always at the head
- `peek()` returns the minimum in O(1); `poll()` removes the minimum in O(log n); `add()` inserts in O(log n)
- Iteration order is NOT sorted – it traverses the heap's internal array, which is only partially ordered
- **Sorted list** (`ArrayList` + `Collections.sort()`) keeps all elements in order but requires O(n) insertion to maintain sort
- **TreeSet** provides O(log n) sorted operations but does not allow duplicates
s1_definition.analogy: PriorityQueue is like a hospital emergency room. The most critical patient is always treated first (min/max at head), but the waiting room is not sorted by severity – patients sit wherever they want. A sorted list is like an alphabetical attendance register where everyone is in order and you can read from A to Z at any time.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  PriorityQueue (min-heap)

  Internal array: [10, 30, 20, 50, 40]

  Heap structure:        10
                       /    \
                     30      20
                    /  \
                  50    40

  peek() → 10 (O(1) – always at root)
  poll() → 10 (O(log n) – swap root with last, sink down)

  After poll(10): [20, 30, 40, 50]
                         20
                       /    \
                     30      40
                    /
                  50

  Iteration: traverses array [10, 30, 20, 50, 40] – NOT sorted!
  Poll loop: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 – sorted!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
PriorityQueue is a min-heap that guarantees only one thing: the smallest element is always at the head. Calling peek() gives you the minimum in O(1), and poll() extracts it in O(log n). But iterating the queue does not give sorted order – it traverses the heap's internal array, which is only partially ordered.

In the National Bank of India's trade processing system, Rajesh uses a PriorityQueue to process high-value transactions first. Each transaction has a priority based on its amount, and the queue always surfaces the highest-priority transaction for the next processing slot. For the monthly trade report that shows all transactions sorted by date, he uses a TreeSet because the entire collection needs to be in sorted order.

The choice is simple: if you need repeated extraction of the min/max element, use PriorityQueue. If you need all elements in sorted order for display or range queries, use TreeSet (unique) or ArrayList with sort (allows duplicates).

Remember one sentence: PriorityQueue guarantees the minimum at the head, not sorted iteration – use poll in a loop for sorted output.
